This 61-year-old woman has ~1 month of anterior neck tenderness, fatigue and reported difficulty swallowing. Exam elicits mild anterior neck (thyroid) tenderness without palpable mass or lymphadenopathy; TSH is normal. Key differentials: thyroiditis (subacute/granulomatous vs silent vs Hashimoto), musculoskeletal neck pain, infectious (suppurative) thyroiditis, and thyroid neoplasm.

Arguments for subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis: classically presents with anterior thyroid pain and tenderness, often in middle-aged to older women, with systemic symptoms (fatigue) and dysphagia/neck discomfort; duration of weeks to months is typical. Although de Quervain often causes transient thyrotoxicosis with low TSH, thyroid function can be in transition (e.g., euthyroid) depending on timing, so a normal TSH does not exclude it. Lack of fever, lymphadenopathy, or leukocytosis makes suppurative infection unlikely. Musculoskeletal pain would more commonly be movement-dependent and less likely to localize as thyroid tenderness or cause swallowing difficulty. Silent (painless) thyroiditis is typically non-tender. Thyroid cancer is usually painless and would often produce a palpable nodule.

Given the focal anterior thyroid tenderness, subacute granulomatous (de Quervain) thyroiditis is the single most likely diagnosis, pending confirmatory labs (ESR/CRP, repeat thyroid function tests, thyroid ultrasound).

However, PVS by definition requires iron‑deficiency anemia together with an esophageal/web-associated dysphagia. No CBC or iron studies (hemoglobin, MCV, ferritin, serum iron/TIBC) were provided, so the key diagnostic element (iron deficiency) is missing.
